Moving slowly, often perched in one place for a while.  Size and shape similar to warbling vireo, maybe a little bigger and a little slower than the normal warbling vireos I see.  It was much browner than most warbling vireos I've seen in the garden and the gray/black cap contrasted more with the supercillium.  White underside.
Same individual observed this morning in a slightly different place in the garden.
Continuing bird first seen yesterday morning.  This time it came down to the upper part of the creek to drink briefly.

We observed the parents tending it, and by watching the parents the next day we found another fledgling (Southpaw) about 15m away. Southpaw was learning to fly by making upward flapping jumps of 10-15 cm, moving branch-to-branch up the bushes and trees a total of 2-3 m before falling back down. Dexter does not have a very good tree/bush to practice in and is learning more slowly. description:
With 25 others; an intensive, two-month bird color-banding/bleeding/resighting study testing the effects of a nematicide (Nemacur) on resident birds in six citrus groves on Merritt Island: five within Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge and one to the south on private property. The project was conducted by Environmental Labs Incorporated (ELI) out of Provo, Utah, for the Mobay Corporation. The Principal Investigator was Ron Parrish, the Quality Control Investigator was David Aborn, and I was the Field Supervisor (I was the only Floridian on the crew!).

All work was done through permits with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.

We used more than 90 mist nets daily to capture landbirds in two groves each day for three consecutive days followed by a day off. This schedule lasted from 2 April through 31 May (a total of 44 banding days), as follows: Day 1: one plot in the refuge and the other plot south of the refuge; Day 2: two plots in the refuge; and Day 3: two plots in the refuge.

I no longer have the specific locations of the six groves, nor which groves we worked on any given day -- the study was 35 years ago and I was not the PI -- so I have drawn a general circle that likely takes in all six groves.

I took all these print photographs and Kodachrome slides and scanned them into JPEGs a decade or more ago.

description:
With Valeri Ponzo; Day 1 of a pretty epic two-day birding trip to Miami-Dade County. I worked a job at Dillard’s in Orlando overnight, ending at 0140, and drove the crew back to Port Richey, arriving at 0518. I ate breakfast at Denny’s to stay awake, then drove to Val’s, arriving at 0729. I (literally!) was asleep by 0730 and Val drove south.

Our itinerary today was:

0729: leave Val's home in Sarasota. I was asleep within 30 seconds, while Val drove.

1113-1350: A.D. "Doug" Barnes Park -- an unsuccessful search for the two lovebirds (at least one a Rosy-faced Lovebird) found here 30 August but apparently not seen afterward. The weather was sunny, hottish/hot, and breezy; we did surprisingly well considering the weather and time of day. We spent most of our time south and east of the swimming pool (where the lovebirds were seen -- and where we found some fruiting figs that attracted several nice Neotropical migrants), but we walked the entire perimeter once. We found our lifer Bark Anoles (Anolis distichus), identified by Jack Crittenden.

1552-1722: Tropical Park -- a visit because we had time to kill and I didn't know where else to go; this was a parrot hotspot in the 1980s (but apparently no longer is). The weather alternated between sunny, hot, and breezy and stormy and windy. We parked near the largest lake and walked around a bit, then noticed the "natural area" and walked the perimeter as much as permitted (a COVID-19 testing site has been set up near the area, and access was blocked off). 

1735-1815: A.D. "Doug" Barnes Park -- our second unsuccessful search of the day for the two lovebirds (at least one a Rosy-faced Lovebird) found here 30 August but apparently not seen afterward. The weather was overcast with light rain for much of the visit. We spent all of our time at the lovebird spot between the swimming pool and the road to the south, so much of the visit was technically out of the park. 

1828-1916_ Brewer Park on Miller Drive -- a successful search for Chestnut-fronted Macaws. The weather was overcast with light sprinkling. We birded the park and walked around the neighborhood surrounding it.

We stayed overnight at Elsa Alvear's home.

description:
With Valeri Ponzo; a successful chase of the Sulphur-bellied Flycatcher at Barnes Park in Miami. I left home at 0413 and arrived at Sarasota at 0607. We were underway in Val's car at 0620, stopping quickly for fuel.

Our itinerary for today (and a bit of tomorrow!) was:

0840-0922: Collier County Rest Area, Big Cypress National Preserve -- a potty break followed by an iNat session. I added two birds to my photographed-in-Collier County list: Blue Jay and Boat-tailed Grackle! We each got at least one lifer: Metallic Blue Lady Beetle (Curinus coeruleus), a very cool-looking "bug."

1033-1418: A.D. (Doug) Barnes Park -- a successful chase of the Sulphur-bellied Flycatcher, which I found perched in a Gumbo Limbo at 1103, so it was a rather easy, rather quick lifer. The weather at the start was post-rain (small pockets of rainwater were in the parking lot), overcast, 81 degrees ("feels like" 87), and breezy. I chased a Sulphur-bellied Flycatcher at Fort De Soto Park in Pinellas County on 28 Sep 2000, but missed it. I had no opportunity to chase another, until today. We saw Tim Towles, and we met Alyssa Crittenden and her dad, Jack. After finding the flycatcher, we remained at Barnes for three more hours, photographing other birds, then walking around, looking for life "bugs" and plants. Although the flycatcher was the star of the show, a Philadelphia Vireo (known to be present) that perched conspicuously less than 20 feet away and then preened for three minutes was another highlight. I added three birds to my Miami-Dade bird list, all of them photographed: Sulphur-bellied Flycatcher, Philadelphia Vireo, and Rose-breasted Grosbeak. We did not see the Yellow-green Vireo recorded previously, and seen by at least one birder today, before we arrived.

1510-1822: Markham Park and Target Range, Sunrise -- I suggested to Val that we visit the butterfly garden because I got my life Soldier here when I most recently visited, on 28 Jan 2024. We spent nearly two hours within 300 feet of the parking area before we entered the butterfly garden or walked the trails (!) -- there were lots of "bugs" here. We walked part of the nature trail, which was unwalkable on the side trails due to a lack of maintenance. White Peacocks were everywhere, and Common Cotton Stainer Bugs were surprisingly numerous. I am sure that we both got several lifer plants and "bugs" here.

1834-2008: The Yard House, Sunrise Mills mall -- we enjoyed an absolutely delicious dinner here -- and I got a new Broward County audio-recorded bird in Fish Crow (there were a few hundred in the mall parking lot as we were entering the restaurant).

2008-2318: driving back to Val's. I missed only one turn all day, an achievement in Broward and Miami-Dade counties!

2328-0138 (Sunday): after fueling up Little Red, I arrived back at Spring Hill.

The Sulphur-bellied Flycatcher is the 549th bird species that I have seen outside of captivity in Florida, and the 527th that I have photographed.

Since the Markham butterfly garden and environs consist of many plants cultivated for butterflies, I tried to be careful in the plants I am submitting. If any of my submissions are known to be planted, please mark as captive.

This is an atypical state park; the gate was locked at 0830 (and remained locked when we left at 1100), there is an "honor" pay station, and there are few facilities -- although the bathrooms were unlocked and clean. We saw nobody else in the park while we were there. The weather at the start was clear and cool with calm winds, becoming sunny and hot with a light breeze at the end. We walked to the canoe launch, then the nature trail north from the paved loop park road. We hit a nice flock of landbirds near the bathrooms, and continued to see birds the entire visit.
